text.title: Migration Impact Mapping Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for mapping a multi-month migration: blast radius counted rather than estimated, a named seam before the first edit, declared expand/contract phases, an explicit point of no return, dual-write reconciliation, the compatibility surface that outlives the deploy, and the trunk-not-branch constraint.

rule.statement: The map MUST state affected files and call sites as counts produced by a reproducible command recorded in the artefact — a language-aware reference search (`ts-morph`, `go/analysis`, `jdeps`, IDE find-usages export) or a stated `rg` pattern — together with the total file count used as the denominator. Adjectives ("large", "most of the service") are rejected. Where the affected share exceeds 30% of files or crosses a runtime boundary, the map MUST route to a staged plan rather than a single cutover.
rule.rationale: Migration estimates are anchored on the files the author has recently opened, and the miss is one-directional: call sites in scripts, tests, config templates and generated code are invisible to memory but block the cutover exactly the same. A recorded command also lets the same count be re-run later as the burn-down metric, which an estimate cannot supply.

rule.statement: Before any migration commit lands, the map MUST name the seam where old and new implementations coexist — the specific module, interface, proxy or route table — and the mechanism that selects between them (feature flag key, routing rule, environment variable). A plan with no named seam is a big-bang rewrite and MUST be labelled as such in the artefact.
rule.rationale: Without a seam, old and new cannot both be live, so the migration cannot be shipped incrementally and cannot be reverted below whole-release granularity. Every intermediate state then exists only on a branch, and the first production signal about the new implementation arrives on the day 100% of traffic moves to it.

rule.statement: For any change to a persisted schema or a published contract, the map MUST list the phases explicitly — expand (add new, keep old) → dual-write → backfill → read-new → contract (drop old) — and mark each phase as independently deployable and individually revertible. Phases MUST NOT be merged in a single deploy.

rationale.source: Parallel change / expand-and-contract (Danilo Sato, Fowler bliki); Evolutionary Database Design

rule.rationale: During a rolling deploy or a canary, old and new code run against one database at the same time. A migration that renames or drops in the same release as the code change gives the not-yet-replaced instances a schema they cannot read, so the error window is the deploy duration, and rollback is impossible because the old column no longer exists.

rule.statement: The map MUST name the exact phase after which rollback stops being possible and only forward-fix remains — typically the contract phase, or the first destructive backfill — and state the gate that MUST pass before crossing it: soak duration at 100% traffic, zero reconciliation drift over the soak, and old-path traffic confirmed at zero. Until that gate passes, the rollback procedure MUST have been executed at least once in a non-production environment.
rule.rationale: Teams assume rollback exists for the whole migration, when in fact it expires quietly the moment the old column is dropped or the legacy consumer is decommissioned. Naming the boundary converts an implicit assumption into a checkable gate, and an untested rollback path is discovered to be broken only under the incident that required it.

rule.statement: Any dual-write phase MUST ship with a reconciliation check before it is enabled: a stated comparison query or job, its run frequency, an explicit drift budget (rows allowed to differ), and an alert when the budget is exceeded. Dual-write with no divergence detector MUST NOT be enabled.
rule.rationale: Two writes to two stores are not one transaction: a crash, a timeout, or a validation rule present in only one store leaves the pair silently divergent, and nothing in the request path notices because the read still comes from the old store. The divergence is discovered at the read-new switch, by which point the backfill is weeks old and there is no record of which rows drifted or when.

rule.statement: The map MUST enumerate everything holding the old format that survives the deploy: serialised rows and JSON blobs, in-flight queue messages, cached values with their TTL, stored procedures and reports, and the oldest client version still in the wild with its forced-upgrade capability. Each entry MUST carry a drain time or a compatibility window. Mobile clients that cannot be force-upgraded are recorded with the store review lag included.
rule.rationale: Deploying replaces running code, not stored data; queue messages written by the old producer and cache entries with a 24-hour TTL keep arriving at the new consumer for as long as the longest TTL after cutover. Shipped mobile clients are the extreme case: the field population never fully converges, so the compatibility window is set by the oldest version still in use, not by the release date.

rule.statement: Migration work MUST land on trunk incrementally behind the seam's flag or route. A long-lived migration branch is forbidden; the map MUST state the maximum branch lifetime (<= 2 days) and the flag key gating the incomplete new path.
rule.rationale: Conflict cost on a divergent branch grows with the product of branch age and trunk churn, and a migration touching more than 30% of files intersects nearly every other change. A three-month branch therefore ends in a merge whose conflict resolution is itself unreviewed, untested work performed under deadline — reintroducing exactly the risk the map was written to bound.
